svg.text: One copy: cp.async goes straight to shared memory
The K tile is 8,192 bytes = 512 pieces of 16 bytes. Each of the block's 128 threads copies 4 pieces of K,
and 4 of V, with one cp.async per piece.
The thread waits for the data,
then stores it. No maths meanwhile.
The thread only starts the copy
Groups: start K, then V straight after, and wait only for K
A thread starts its instructions one at a time, in order, but does not wait for one to finish before starting
the next. So it starts K's copies, then V's right after, and both move at the same time. commit_group puts the
copies started so far into one group. wait_group(n) pauses the thread until at most n of its groups are still moving.

svg.text: V's 4 copies become group 2. Both groups
now move at once; still no waiting.

text.font-family: ui-monospace, 'SF Mono', Menlo, Consolas, 'DejaVu Sans Mono', monospace

svg.text: 2 groups moving: it waits until only 1 is left.
The THREAD pauses; K and V keep moving.
K lands, so only 1 group (V) is still moving.
The thread goes on to the next instruction.
The barrier waits for threads, not copies, so V
keeps moving, and lands while the thread uses K.

text.font-family: ui-monospace, 'SF Mono', Menlo, Consolas, 'DejaVu Sans Mono', monospace

svg.text: wait_group(0), barrier, then O += P V
V has landed, so wait_group(0) lets it calculate
with V. K is done; its space can take the next K.
K and V are the same size, so each moves for 3 steps; V is one step behind because it was started one step later.
n is how many of the newest groups may still be moving; every older group must be done. So wait_group(1) means "K done,
V may still be moving". wait_group(0) would wait for every group. So the group the thread needs first must be the
oldest one: that is why K is started first. The three timelines below compare the choices.
Why two groups, and why K first? Three ways to load K and V
One group for K and V

svg.text: S = Q Kᵀ waits for V too,
although it does not use V.

svg.text: Now K is the newest group, so it
lands last, and the only way to wait
for it is wait_group(0). No better

text.font-family: ui-monospace, 'SF Mono', Menlo, Consolas, 'DejaVu Sans Mono', monospace

svg.text: S = Q Kᵀ starts as soon as K
K and V are the same size (8 KB per tile), so their bars are the same length. The one started second lands a little later, because its
copies queue behind the first one's. That gap is the time the K-first order saves: small when memory is idle, larger when it is busy.
Barrier: wait for every thread's copies
wait_group only knows about this thread's own copies. The other 127 threads copied the rest of the tile.
its own K pieces have landed;
4 threads shown. Every thread did its own wait_group before reaching the barrier, so all 512 pieces of K have landed.
